notes: \cpara{Recalls that at nine the author, a reader of Feynman's \textsc{QED}, ``knew'' that light, sound and matter were waves.}

\cfact{The post does not say that \textsc{QED} taught this. The book says in its first lecture: ``It is very important to know that light behaves like particles, especially for those of you who have gone to school, where you were probably told something about light behaving like waves.'' Later it says that light and electrons both ``behave somewhat like waves, and somewhat like particles.''}
\cpara{Tells how three days with the wave equation in the \textsc{Feynman Lectures on Physics} showed the author that the younger self had had no idea what ``wave'' meant to a physicist.}
\cpara{Sets up the question: if we accept ``waves'' from a physicist, is it unfair to reject it from a student?}
\cpara{The post's answer: words have no intrinsic definitions, so the student's ``Waves!'' is only verbal behavior, and treating it as true or false is a habit learned at school.}

\clogic{The answer rests on a view of meaning that the post does not defend. On a standard view, Hilary Putnam's ``division of linguistic labor'' (1975) and Tyler Burge's argument (1979), a speaker who uses a word as experts do, and would accept their correction, means what the experts mean. On that view the student's ``Waves!'' says what the physicist's says, and what the student lacks is understanding. The post's lesson needs only the second claim.}
\cpara{Brings back the metal plate of ``Fake Explanations,'' now in school: ``I don't know'' earns nothing, so the student offers one of the teacher's phrases.}
\cpara{Names the practice: guessing the teacher's password.}

\cfact{Feynman described the same thing in ``O Americano, Outra Vez!'' (\textsc{Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!}, 1985). Brazilian physics students could define Brewster's angle but did not recognize it in light reflected from the bay: ``the students had memorized everything, but they didn't know what anything meant.'' The post names two of Feynman's books, not this passage.}
\cpara{Sets the test: an equation is connected to experience only when you use it to predict the next measurement. Even a picture of heat flowing counts, if it leads to a test with a match.}
\cpara{Says that without using the equation, what remains is ``verbal behavior,'' not belief.}

\clogic{Loosely worded. The paragraph before says that a student who ``just visualizes something flowing'' and tests it with a match, without the equation, is connected to experience. Read literally, this sentence says that student's connection is severed.}
\cpara{Restates, without evidence, that school grades only verbal behavior, and says unlearning this begins with telling an explanation from a password.}
\cpara{Grants that ``heat conduction?'' may be a first step, if it is not treated as a password, and says the author fell into the trap at nine.}
\cstyle{``Wakalixes'' is Feynman's word, from the passage noted at ``Fake Explanations''; it is not explained here.}

\clogic{One case, the author at nine, supports ``this is what happens by default'' and a claim about all of humanity. The post gives no historical example; the next day's ``Fake Causality'' supplies one, phlogiston.}

\cpara{The remedy, offered with ``Maybe'': teach that only anticipation-controllers count, so that ``heat conduction?'' leads to a sequence of questions and tests. It is the post's fullest example of its method.}
\cpara{Ends by repeating, in italics, the tenth paragraph's claim about the whole human species.}
